For rotation: hashicorp/time provider (time_rotating resource) is proper idempotent approach. formatdate(format, timestamp()): format timestamp.

questions.question: A `templatefile` rendering a YAML document needs each line of a MULTI-LINE INPUT string indented under a parent key. `indent(2, multi_line_str)` adds 2 spaces to every line EXCEPT the first. Useful for embedding multi-line strings inside YAML / JSON templates. Which describes it?
options: Adds N spaces to the beginning of each line
Code formatting — partial; `indent(N, str)` adds N spaces to the beginning of each line of a multi-line string; it does not reformat HCL syntax like `terraform fmt` does
questions.explanation: indent(num_spaces, string): adds N spaces to each line except first. Use in templatefile: 'config:\n${indent(2, var.complex_config)}'. Produces properly indented output. Common with yamlencode/jsonencode: embed formatted sub-objects inside larger template files. Rarely needed in normal Terraform use but valuable for configuration generation.

questions.question: A list `["a", "", null, "b"]` should be reduced to `["a", "b"]` (drop nulls + empty strings). `compact(list)` does this. Useful after collection-shaping operations that may leave gaps. Which describes it?
options: Removes null and empty string values
questions.explanation: compact: compact(['first', '', var.optional_value, 'last']) — removes empty strings and nulls. Use when building lists with conditional elements: [var.name, var.optional_suffix == '' ? '' : '-${var.optional_suffix}'] then wrap in compact. Works only on list of strings (not numbers or mixed types).

questions.question: An expression `regexall("[0-9]+", "foo123bar456")` returns `["123", "456"]`. Unlike `regex` (which returns ONE match), `regexall` returns a LIST of all matches. Useful for extracting all IPs / IDs / numbers from a string. Which describes it?
options: Returns LIST of all matches of a regex
questions.explanation: regexall: returns list (empty if no matches, never errors). length(regexall('[a-z]+', var.name)) > 0: check if name contains lowercase. regex: returns first match or errors. can(regex(pattern, string)): safe match test. Variable validation: condition = can(regex('^[a-z][a-z0-9-]*$', var.name)). Used for: input validation, pattern extraction.

questions.question: A map `{c=3, a=1, b=2}` needs its KEYS as a sorted list (`["a","b","c"]`) and VALUES in matching order (`[1,2,3]`). `keys(map)` returns SORTED keys; `values(map)` returns values in KEY-sorted order. The pair preserves the key-value correspondence. Which describes them?
questions.explanation: keys/values: keys({a=1, b=2}) = ['a','b']. values({a=1, b=2}) = [1,2]. Keys sorted alphabetically (consistent ordering). for_each = toset(keys(var.users)): iterate map by key. for k, v in var.users: direct iteration. zipmap(keys_list, values_list): rebuild map. transpose(map): swap keys and values (for maps of lists).

questions.question: A variable should accept only DNS-safe names (lowercase, alphanumeric, hyphen, 3-20 chars). The validation pattern uses `can()` to guard regex evaluation: `condition = can(regex("^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{2,19}$", var.name))`. If the regex matches, `regex` returns the match (truthy); if not, errors → `can()` catches → false → validation fails. Which describes the pattern?
questions.explanation: Best practice for regex validation: variable 'cluster_name' { validation { condition = can(regex('^[a-z][a-z0-9-]*$', var.cluster_name)), error_message = 'Name must start with lowercase letter, contain only lowercase alphanumeric and hyphens' } }. can(regex()) pattern: idiomatic Terraform validation. More readable than regexall([...]) length check.

questions.question: Each Terraform workspace has its OWN state file. Resources / outputs / data in workspace A are invisible to workspace B. They DO share the configuration code (same .tf files). State isolation is per-workspace: local backend stores in `terraform.tfstate.d/<name>/`; remote backends use prefixed keys. Which describes state isolation?
options: Each workspace has a completely separate state file
questions.explanation: Workspace state isolation: fundamentally separate states. Same configuration, different state = different infrastructure instances (dev database and prod database). terraform.workspace in code: customize per workspace. Variable values: set per workspace in Terraform Cloud, or use separate .tfvars files per workspace.

questions.question: A reusable module declares it ACCEPTS multiple provider configurations of the same type (e.g., a multi-region module taking `aws.east` + `aws.west`). The module's `terraform { required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws"; configuration_aliases = [aws.east, aws.west] } } }` declares this. The root module then PASSES the provider configurations via `providers = { aws.east = aws.east, aws.west = aws.west }`. Which describes configuration_aliases?
questions.explanation: configuration_aliases: module defines required_providers { aws = { source='hashicorp/aws', configuration_aliases=[aws.us-east, aws.eu-west] } }. Root module: module 'multi_region' { providers = { aws.us-east = aws.us-east, aws.eu-west = aws.eu-west } }. Module resources use provider = aws.us-east. Enables clean multi-region module design.

questions.question: A CI/CD pipeline runs `terraform plan` and needs to KNOW whether the plan contains changes — to skip apply if there are none, or fail-fast on errors. Without intervention `plan` always exits 0 (success). The `-detailed-exitcode` flag changes this: 0 = no changes, 1 = error, 2 = success with changes. Which describes it?
questions.explanation: -detailed-exitcode: standard exit=0 (success/no-changes or success/changes — can't distinguish). Detailed: 0=no changes, 1=error, 2=changes needed. CI script: terraform plan -detailed-exitcode; if [ $? -eq 2 ]; then terraform apply; fi. Automates: skip apply when no changes needed. Common in GitOps pipelines.

questions.question: A `data "aws_subnet" "x"` query may return ambiguous results. Terraform 1.3+ allows a `lifecycle { precondition { condition = …; error_message = … } }` block INSIDE the data source — validates assumptions BEFORE the data source is read. Useful for guarding subnet count / IP availability / etc. Which describes it?
questions.explanation: Data source preconditions: validate inputs before querying provider. Fail fast with useful error messages rather than confusing provider API errors. Example: ensure search criteria will return valid results. Postconditions: validate returned data meets expectations (e.g., AMI must be EBS-backed, must be encrypted). Terraform 1.2+.

questions.question: Inside a MODULE, a resource `aws_instance.web` was renamed to `aws_instance.app`. To AVOID destroy + create on apply, the module author adds a `moved { from = aws_instance.web; to = aws_instance.app }` block inside the module. Terraform state is updated in place at next plan. The block also works at root level. Which describes moved in modules?
options: Declares that a resource (or whole module)
questions.explanation: Module-level moved: rename a module in root config without recreating resources. module.database (old) → module.rds (new): add moved { from=module.database, to=module.rds }. Apply: state updated (resource addresses renamed), no infrastructure changes. Remove moved block after all consumers have applied. Terraform 1.1+.

questions.question: A configuration reads `policy.json` (an AWS IAM policy as JSON) and passes it to an `aws_iam_policy.policy_json` attribute. `jsondecode(file("policy.json"))` parses the JSON into HCL values; `jsonencode(local.policy_obj)` does the reverse — produces a JSON string from HCL. Useful for IAM policies, K8s manifests, custom config. Which describes the pair?
questions.explanation: jsonencode: jsonencode({Version='2012-10-17', Statement=[{Effect='Allow', Action='*', Resource='*'}]}). Creates valid JSON for IAM policies, container definitions, etc. jsondecode: jsondecode(data.aws_iam_policy_document.main.json) → Terraform map. Cleaner than heredoc JSON strings. Validate JSON syntax at plan time (not runtime).

questions.question: A team consumes a MODULE published in a private git repository. The `source` argument supports git URLs: `git::https://github.com/org/repo.git?ref=v1.0` (HTTPS + tag) or `git::ssh://git@github.com/org/repo.git?ref=feature/x` (SSH + branch). `ref` can be tag, branch, or commit SHA. Which describes git sources?
questions.explanation: Git module sources: always pin ref (don't use HEAD/main — unstable). Prefer tags (semantic versioning) for production modules. SSH vs HTTPS: SSH requires key setup (good for CI), HTTPS requires token or PAC. Subdirectory: useful for monorepos with multiple modules. Private repos: configure git credentials before terraform init.

questions.question: Two equal-length lists `["env","team"]` (keys) and `["prod","web"]` (values) must become the map `{env="prod", team="web"}`. Which function pairs them?
options: `merge(keys, values)` — merges two maps into one
`setproduct(keys, values)` — pairs every key with every value
`zipmap(keys, values)` — builds a map by pairing two equal-length lists
`lookup(map, key)` — returns a single value from a map
questions.explanation: zipmap pairs the keys list with the values list positionally into a map. merge takes maps, not key/value lists. setproduct returns the Cartesian product (every combination), not a 1:1 pairing. lookup retrieves one value from an existing map and does not build one.

questions.question: A new Terraform language construct is provisional and may change or be removed in a future release. How do you opt into it, accepting the stability risk?
options: Install a `-beta` pre-release build of the Terraform CLI
Add the feature to `required_providers` with a pre-release version
questions.explanation: Language experiments are opted into per configuration with experiments = [...] in the terraform block on a normal CLI release. There is no separate beta CLI for language features, required_providers governs provider versions (not language features), and no TF_EXPERIMENTAL env var enables them.

questions.question: Terraform's SET operations: `setintersection(a,b,c)` returns elements common to ALL sets. `setunion(a,b,c)` returns elements in ANY set. `setsubtract(a,b)` returns `a - b` (elements in a but not in b). Useful for derived sets (e.g., available subnets = all - used). Which describes them?
questions.explanation: Set math: setintersection: elements in ALL sets. setunion: elements in ANY set. setsubtract: elements in first but not second. Use cases: find users in group A AND group B (intersection), all users in either group (union), users to remove (subtract current from desired). Useful with toset() for processing lists as sets.

questions.question: A `name = null` argument on a resource tells Terraform 'use the provider's default for this attribute' — distinct from `name = ""` (empty string) which is a real value. `null` is a special value indicating ABSENCE. Used in conditional expressions: `tag = var.set ? "yes" : null`. Which describes null?
questions.explanation: null: explicitly omit optional attributes. some_resource { optional_attr = var.value == '' ? null : var.value }. When attribute = null: Terraform omits it from API call (provider uses default). Different from '' (empty string). Use for: optional nested blocks, conditional attribute inclusion. Ternary with null: common pattern for optional configurations. Set attribute to null: removes that attribute from API call (use provider default). In conditional: var.optional_attr == null ? null : var.optional_attr. Useful for optional attributes: some_attr = var.override != null ? var.override : null

questions.question: A security team wants to scan Terraform code for misconfigurations — public S3 buckets, 0.0.0.0/0 SSH ingress, IAM policies with `Action: *` — BEFORE running `terraform apply`. Which tool is built for this?
options: Checkov, an open-source static-analysis scanner with 1000+ built-in policies
`terraform validate`, which checks configuration syntax and internal consistency
`terraform plan`, which previews the resource changes Terraform will make
`terraform fmt`, which rewrites configuration files to the canonical style
questions.explanation: Checkov is a dedicated static-analysis tool that scans Terraform (and CloudFormation, Kubernetes, Dockerfiles) against hundreds of security policies and fails the build on misconfigurations. terraform validate only checks that the configuration is syntactically valid and internally consistent — it knows nothing about security posture. terraform plan shows the diff of resources to be changed, not policy violations. terraform fmt only normalises formatting.

questions.question: Two conversion functions: `tolist(set)` converts an unordered set to an ordered list (alphabetical / canonical order). `toset(list)` converts a list to an unordered set (dedup + lose order). Used to convert between collection types when functions demand a specific input. Which describes them?
questions.explanation: Pattern: for_each = toset(var.names) — deduplicate and enable for_each. tolist(aws_instance.web[*].id) — convert tuple to list. toset(['a','b','a']) = {'a','b'} (deduped). tolist({'a','b'}) = ['a','b'] (arbitrary order). Use toset for for_each patterns. Use tolist when you need ordered access by index.

questions.question: A Terraform module's STANDARD file layout: `main.tf` (resources + data sources), `variables.tf` (inputs declared), `outputs.tf` (exports), `versions.tf` (terraform + required_providers), `README.md` (docs + usage example), optionally `locals.tf`, `data.tf`. Splitting by purpose makes the module readable; Terraform reads all .tf files in the directory regardless. Which describes the standard layout?
options: Single main.tf — works but discouraged for non-trivial modules
questions.explanation: Conventional structure: main.tf (core resources), variables.tf (all variable declarations), outputs.tf (all outputs), versions.tf (required_providers, required_version, provider config). examples/ directory: working example usage. tests/ directory: .tftest.hcl files. README: generated by terraform-docs. CHANGELOG: semantic versioning history. Consistency enables tooling (terraform-docs, semantic-release). variables.tf (input variables), outputs.tf (output values), versions.tf (required_providers and required_version), README.md (usage docs), CHANGELOG.md (version history). Optional: locals.tf, data.tf, provider.tf. Subdirectory for examples/ and tests/

questions.question: Before it was deprecated, `terraform taint` mutated state to do what on the next apply — the behaviour now served by `apply -replace`?
options: Prevented a resource from being modified or destroyed
Marked a resource for forced destroy-and-recreate on the next apply
Removed the resource from state without touching real infrastructure
Refreshed the resource's attributes from the provider
questions.explanation: taint flagged a resource so the next apply would destroy and recreate it — now done explicitly with apply -replace. Preventing changes is lifecycle prevent_destroy. Removing from state without deleting infra is state rm. Refreshing attributes is refresh — none of which force a replacement.

questions.question: Modern Terraform's replacement for `terraform taint`: `terraform apply -replace=<address>` (also `plan -replace`). It doesn't mutate state until apply; the plan visibly shows DESTROY + CREATE for the specified resource. Multiple `-replace` flags can be passed. Which describes it?
options: destroy -target then apply — works but two operations + risk; -replace is the canonical one-shot
questions.explanation: terraform apply -replace=google_compute_instance.web: shows plan with resource marked for replacement, then executes. More transparent than taint (shows the replacement plan before confirming). Use when a specific resource needs to be recreated without destroying everything else.

questions.question: `null_resource` is a resource that implements the standard Terraform lifecycle (create / destroy / triggers) but DOES NOT create real infrastructure. Used as a hook for `local-exec` / `remote-exec` provisioners, or as a synthetic resource for `depends_on` / `triggers`. Terraform 1.4+ introduces `terraform_data` as a cleaner replacement for many use cases. Which describes it?
options: A resource that implements the standard
questions.explanation: null_resource: triggers = {} map to control when it re-runs. Provisioner executes on create (or destroy). Use cases: run a script after infrastructure is created, create a dependency between resources without a direct reference, trigger provisioners conditionally. terraform-provider-null required.

questions.question: A configuration needs UNIQUE random suffixes for resource names (avoid name collisions across re-applies). `hashicorp/random` provider provides `random_id`, `random_string`, `random_password`, `random_uuid`, `random_pet`, `random_shuffle` resources. Values are generated ONCE at create + stored in state (stable across applies until destroy / recreate). Which describes it?
questions.explanation: random_string: generates random alphanumeric string. random_id: generates random bytes in hex/base64. random_password: generates strong password. random_integer: random number in range. These resources are stable after creation (don't regenerate on each apply unless keepers change). integers, UUIDs, passwords) within Terraform configurations — commonly used for: unique resource names (S3 buckets, database passwords), avoiding naming conflicts, generating entropy for resources that require unique IDs

questions.question: Provisioning a managed DB takes ~5 min for the cluster to fully become available — the resource is 'created' but not yet 'usable'. A downstream resource that depends on the DB might fail. The `time_sleep` resource (from `hashicorp/time` provider) introduces a configurable delay between resource creations: `resource "time_sleep" "wait_5m" { depends_on = [aws_db_instance.main]; create_duration = "5m" }`. Which describes it?
questions.explanation: time_sleep.wait_30_seconds { create_duration = '30s' depends_on = [aws_instance.db] }. Other resources depend on this sleep. Use sparingly — prefer proper readiness checks. time_static: captures current time as a static value for tagging/versioning. creates a delay between resource creation steps. Use when: a resource needs time to become available after creation (e.g., wait 30s after creating a database before creating a dependent service)

questions.question: An expression `sensitive(var.password)` returns the same value but MARKED SENSITIVE in plan output (redacted to '(sensitive value)'). Useful when a value isn't statically marked sensitive but should be redacted for a specific use. Different from `nonsensitive` (which unmarks). Which describes `sensitive`?
questions.explanation: sensitive(): wraps any value to mark it sensitive. Terraform redacts it in plan output (shows as '(sensitive value)'). Note: the value IS still stored in state — sensitive() only affects display. For real secrets: use Vault provider or AWS Secrets Manager to retrieve at runtime, never store in state.

questions.question: A `variable` block needs to reject any value the caller passes that isn't an SSH-compatible CIDR (must match the regex `^\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+\/\d+$`). The check should run at plan time and fail with a clear message before any resource is touched. Which Terraform feature implements this?
options: An `assert` block at the root module level — `assert` is not a valid top-level Terraform block; the correct way to enforce a constraint with a custom error_message on a variable is a `validation` block inside the variable declaration
A `validation { condition = … error_message = … }` block on the variable
A `precondition` block inside every resource that reads the variable
A `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` block, which validates inputs
questions.explanation: Variable-level validation lives inside the variable block itself: `validation { condition = can(regex("^…", var.cidr)); error_message = "…" }`. It fires at plan time. There is no `assert` block. `precondition`/`postcondition` are lifecycle features for resources and outputs (1.2+) and don't gate variable values directly. `prevent_destroy` only blocks destroy operations.

questions.question: Terraform 1.5+ introduces an `import { to = aws_s3_bucket.legacy; id = "my-bucket" }` BLOCK in .tf files. The block is planned + applied as part of normal Terraform workflow. Replaces the imperative `terraform import` CLI workflow with a code-first approach that's version-controllable + reviewable. Can also `terraform plan -generate-config-out=` to generate the missing resource block. Which describes it?
questions.explanation: import { to = aws_instance.example, id = 'i-1234567890' }. Run terraform plan: shows what will be imported. terraform apply: performs import. -generate-config-out=generated.tf: auto-generates resource configuration from imported resource. Much better than CLI import for team workflows. defines which existing resources to import into state. Unlike terraform import CLI command, import blocks are plan-able and reviewable before execution. Generate config with -generate-config-out flag

questions.question: A `check` block at root configuration level runs ASSERTIONS about infrastructure AFTER apply (not blocking — produces warnings, not errors). Example: assert `data.http.lb_health.status_code == 200`. The check runs on every plan/apply. Different from preconditions (which block resource creation). Which describes check blocks?
questions.explanation: check 'website_reachable' { data 'http' 'healthcheck' { url = 'https://example.com' } assert { condition = data.http.healthcheck.status_code == 200 error_message = 'Website returned unexpected status.' } }. Run every plan/apply. Failures are warnings, not errors. Continuous compliance checking.

questions.question: A configuration needs to render a TEMPLATE FILE (`config.yaml.tmpl`) substituting `${var}` placeholders with HCL values. Output: a fully-rendered string suitable for cloud-init user-data, K8s manifest generation, etc. The `templatefile(path, vars)` function reads the file + renders. Which describes it?
questions.explanation: templatefile('scripts/init.sh.tpl', { db_host = aws_db_instance.main.address, env = var.environment }). Template file uses ${var} syntax. Useful for user_data in EC2, cloud-init scripts, config files. Alternative to heredoc strings in resource config.

questions.question: A monorepo has many subdirectories, each with .tf files. The team wants to FORMAT them all in one shot from the repo root. `terraform fmt` only formats the current directory; the `-recursive` flag descends into subdirectories. Which describes it?
questions.explanation: terraform fmt: enforces canonical style. -recursive: all subdirectories. -check: return non-zero if files need formatting (for CI/CD gates). -diff: show what would change. Always run before commits in team projects. Formatting is deterministic — same code always formats the same way.

questions.question: A `moved { from = aws_instance.web; to = module.web_tier.aws_instance.web }` block tells Terraform: this resource has been RENAMED in the configuration (often moved into a module). Terraform updates state in place at next plan — no destroy + create. Modernised alternative to the imperative `terraform state mv`. Which describes the moved block?
options: Declares that a resource was renamed or
questions.explanation: moved { from = aws_instance.old_name, to = aws_instance.new_name }. Run terraform plan: shows 'moved' instead of destroy/create. Apply: updates state. moved blocks can also move resources into/out of modules. Remove moved blocks after all team members have applied the change.

questions.question: Two separate Terraform configurations share infrastructure: STACK A creates a VPC; STACK B deploys ECS into it and needs VPC's id. Stack B uses `data "terraform_remote_state" "vpc" { backend = "s3"; config = { … } }` to read STACK A's outputs from its remote state file. Which describes the data source?
questions.explanation: data 'terraform_remote_state' 'vpc' { backend = 's3', config = { bucket = 'my-state', key = 'vpc/terraform.tfstate' } }. Access outputs: data.terraform_remote_state.vpc.outputs.vpc_id. Creates coupling between stacks — consider carefully. Alternative: use shared data sources (AWS SSM, Consul) for looser coupling.

questions.question: Two related Terraform concepts: (A) Terraform CLI workspace — a named instance of state inside a single backend (e.g. `default`, `dev`, `prod`); switched with `terraform workspace select`. (B) Terraform Cloud workspace — a TFC-level isolation boundary with its own variables, run history, state file, and RBAC. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?
options: CLI workspaces are named instances of state within one backend
CLI workspaces require Terraform Cloud as their backend to function
Workspaces (CLI and Cloud) have both been deprecated in Terraform 1.x
questions.explanation: CLI workspaces share the same backend and only swap which state file is active — handy for quick env-per-state, but easy to apply to the wrong one. Cloud workspaces are first-class isolation: each has its own variables, runs, history, RBAC, and VCS link. When using TFC as the backend, `terraform workspace` commands map onto TFC workspaces, but the two concepts are not interchangeable.

questions.question: Two meta-arguments to create multiple instances of a resource. `count = N` produces N instances indexed by [0..N-1]; removing from the middle renumbers + recreates tail. `for_each = { … }` (map) or `toset([…])` (set) produces instances keyed by string; removing a specific key only removes that one instance. for_each is generally safer for changing collections. Which describes the difference?
questions.explanation: for_each { 'us-east-1' = 'ami-123', 'eu-west-1' = 'ami-456' }: resource identified by map key. Remove middle item: only that specific resource destroyed. count [0,1,2]: remove index 1 → index 2 becomes 1 → Terraform sees index 1 changed → destroys+recreates old index 2. Always use for_each for collections. creates one resource per map key/set value with a meaningful identifier. count uses numeric index — fragile when list items are inserted/removed (shifts indices, causes unexpected destroys). for_each preferred for collections

questions.question: Terraform Cloud supports a VCS-driven workflow. A TFC workspace is connected to a GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket repository. Pull requests trigger speculative plans whose output is posted as a PR comment; merges to the default branch trigger applies (auto or with a manual gate). Drift detection runs on a schedule. Which describes this workflow?
options: Apply runs only when CLI is invoked locally
TFC's CLI-only workflow — apply happens on each developer's machine
TFC's VCS-driven workflow — PRs speculatively plan, merges apply
TFC's API-driven workflow — only available when calling the runs endpoint
questions.explanation: VCS-driven is one of three TFC run-trigger modes alongside CLI-driven and API-driven. The defining property is that runs are triggered automatically by repository events: a PR opens → speculative plan, a merge to main → apply. Drift detection adds a scheduled plan on top. CLI-driven workflows trigger from `terraform apply` on a laptop; API-driven from a direct call to the runs endpoint.

questions.question: A module needs to manage AWS resources in TWO regions. Without intervention only ONE `aws` provider config exists. Solution: `provider "aws" { alias = "east"; region = "us-east-1" }` + `provider "aws" { alias = "west"; region = "eu-west-1" }`. Resources opt in via `provider = aws.east`. Modules accept provider configs via `configuration_aliases`. Which describes provider aliases?
questions.explanation: provider 'aws' { alias = 'us_east', region = 'us-east-1' }. provider 'aws' { alias = 'eu_west', region = 'eu-west-1' }. Resource: resource 'aws_instance' 'east' { provider = aws.us_east }. Module: module 'network' { providers = { aws = aws.eu_west } }. Essential for multi-region architectures.

questions.question: An engineer wants to test an HCL expression interactively WITHOUT running plan / apply: `length(var.subnets)`, `cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 1)`, `aws_vpc.main.cidr_block`. Terraform's REPL lets them: type expressions + see their evaluated values immediately, against the current state. Which command?
questions.explanation: terraform console: interactive prompt. Type expressions: cidrsubnet('10.0.0.0/16', 8, 3) → shows result. Test: contains(['a','b'], 'a') → true. Access state: data.aws_vpc.main.id → shows actual ID. Load specific vars: terraform console -var-file=dev.tfvars. Exit with Ctrl+D or exit.

questions.question: Terraform 1.10+ introduces EPHEMERAL VALUES — values that exist only during a single Terraform operation, NEVER persisted to state or plan files. Used for secrets that must be fetched fresh each run (rotated short-lived tokens, vault-leased credentials). Declared via `ephemeral` blocks; used like data sources. Which describes the feature?
questions.explanation: Ephemeral values (TF 1.10+): sensitive data flows through operations without persisting anywhere. Ephemeral resources: created and destroyed within a single Terraform operation (e.g., retrieve Vault token, use it, Vault revokes it). Complementary to existing sensitive() function which still stores in state.

questions.question: A platform team builds complex infrastructure by COMPOSING focused modules: a `vpc` module, `eks` module, `rds` module, `monitoring` module — each handles ONE concern with clean inputs / outputs. Composition (not inheritance) is the canonical Terraform pattern. Modules can call other modules. Which describes composition?
options: Building complex infrastructure by composing multiple FOCUSED
questions.explanation: Root module uses: module 'network' { source = './modules/network' } module 'compute' { source = './modules/compute', vpc_id = module.network.vpc_id }. Modules pass outputs to other modules. Flat module structure preferred over deep nesting. Each module: focused, independently testable, documented.

questions.question: Two state-related files. `terraform.tfstate` — current state of infrastructure (live source of truth used by plan / apply). `terraform.tfstate.backup` — automatic copy of the PREVIOUS state, written before each state-mutating operation. One level of automatic backup. Restore via copying. Which describes them?
questions.explanation: State backup: created automatically before every apply. One backup per state file. If apply fails midway, state may be partially updated — backup helps restore. For team use: remote backends handle state with locking and versioning automatically. Local state: only for solo dev or learning.

questions.question: A Terraform configuration needs the `id` and `cidr_block` of an AWS VPC that was created outside Terraform, and must NOT create, update, or destroy that VPC. Which construct fits?
options: A `data` source, which reads attributes of existing infrastructure without managing it
A `resource` block with `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` to track it read-only
An `import` block, which brings the existing VPC under Terraform management
An `output` value that references the VPC's attributes from the state file
questions.explanation: A data source (data "aws_vpc" "x" { ... }) queries the provider for an existing object and exposes its attributes (data.aws_vpc.x.id) without ever creating, updating, or destroying it. A resource block — even with prevent_destroy — still manages the object and would try to create it. An import block deliberately brings the VPC under management, the opposite of the requirement. An output only re-exports values already in state; it cannot read infrastructure that Terraform does not track.

questions.question: Terraform 0.13+ requires every NON-DEFAULT provider to be declared in `terraform { required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws"; version = "~> 5.0" } } }`. Without this, Terraform can't disambiguate `aws` between providers in different namespaces (`hashicorp/aws` vs `community/aws`). Required for reproducible builds + supply-chain safety. Which describes it?
questions.explanation: terraform { required_providers { aws = { source = 'hashicorp/aws', version = '~> 5.0' } } }. Version constraints: ~> 5.0 (5.x but not 6.0), >= 4.0 (any 4.0+), = 5.1.0 (exact). Always specify. Run terraform providers lock to generate .terraform.lock.hcl with exact checksums for reproducibility.

questions.question: An EC2 instance has `tags = { Name = var.name; ManagedBy = "terraform" }`. Out-of-band a colleague adds a third tag via the AWS console. Terraform plan shows DRIFT + wants to remove the new tag. To IGNORE this specific drift: `lifecycle { ignore_changes = [tags] }`. Terraform stops detecting drift on the listed attributes (still tracks them, but doesn't act on changes). Which describes it?
options: Tells Terraform to IGNORE changes to specific
questions.explanation: lifecycle { ignore_changes = [tags, user_data] }. Terraform still creates/destroys the resource but won't update it when these attributes change outside Terraform. Use carefully — ignoring too much defeats the purpose of IaC. ignore_changes = all: never update (use for imported resources temporarily).

questions.question: An `aws_security_group` needs one `ingress` nested block per allowed port, driven by a `var.allowed_ports` list, without hard-coding each block. Which feature generates the repeated nested blocks?
options: `count` on the security group, creating one group per port
A `dynamic` block, which generates repeated nested blocks from a collection
`for_each` on the security group resource itself
A `for` expression returned directly as the `ingress` argument
questions.explanation: A dynamic block iterates a collection to emit repeated nested blocks (ingress) inside one resource. count and for_each on the resource would create multiple security groups, not multiple ingress blocks within one. A for expression produces a value (list/map) and cannot emit configuration blocks.

questions.question: A regulated bank uses Terraform Cloud and must enforce policies AT PLAN TIME: no public S3 buckets, no instances larger than xlarge, mandatory tagging. Plans that violate policy must HARD-FAIL before reaching apply. The solution: Sentinel — HashiCorp's policy-as-code framework (Terraform Cloud / Enterprise feature) — write `.sentinel` policies that gate plan output. Which describes Sentinel?
questions.explanation: Sentinel: policies run after plan, before apply. Hard-mandatory: block apply if policy fails. Soft-mandatory: allow override with explanation. Advisory: warn only. Use cases: require all resources tagged, block creation in certain regions, enforce instance type limits. Sentinel language: Python-like, purpose-built for policy.

questions.question: A `local.azs = ["us-east-1a", "", "us-east-1b", null, "us-east-1c"]` accidentally contains nulls + empty strings from upstream data. To get a clean `["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b", "us-east-1c"]` in one call: `compact(local.azs)`. Which describes the function?
questions.explanation: compact(['a', '', 'b', null, 'c']) → ['a', 'b', 'c']. Common use: concat() produces nulls from conditional values, compact() cleans them. Example: compact([var.enable_feature ? 'feature-flag' : null, 'always-included']). Use with flatten() for nested list cleaning.

questions.question: A Terraform configuration needs to (a) send a structured tag map to AWS Lambda as a JSON-encoded environment variable, and (b) read a JSON-formatted output from a `data "external"` script back into a Terraform map. Which pair of built-in functions does this?
options: `yamlencode` and `yamldecode` are required because env vars must be YAML
`templatefile()` with a JSON template handles both encoding and parsing
questions.explanation: `jsonencode(value)` converts a Terraform value into a JSON string — perfect for env vars, IAM policy strings, or templated config files. `jsondecode(string)` does the reverse: parse a JSON string into HCL types you can index normally. The direction is easy to mix up, which is why a reversed pair is the most plausible distractor. `yamlencode/yamldecode` exist but are for YAML, and `templatefile()` is for substitution, not parsing.

questions.question: After HashiCorp moved Terraform from MPL to the BSL (Business Source License) in August 2023, the community forked the last MPL-licensed release. The fork: OpenTofu — Linux Foundation project, drop-in CLI-compatible alternative, MPL-licensed. Most providers + modules work on both. Which describes the relationship?
questions.explanation: OpenTofu forked from Terraform 1.5.x (last MPL-2.0 version). Maintained by Linux Foundation, community-governed. Compatible: same .tf syntax, same providers (initially). Adding features: provider-defined functions, state encryption. Use if: license change is a concern, need fully OSS toolchain. HashiCorp Terraform continues development separately.

questions.question: A Terraform Cloud plan introduces 12 EC2 instances + 3 RDS databases. Before approving the apply, the team wants to KNOW THE MONTHLY COST DELTA. Terraform Cloud's Cost Estimation feature analyses plan output, integrates with cloud-provider pricing, and posts a $/month diff alongside the plan. Combine with a Sentinel policy that fails on > $X delta. Which describes the feature?
questions.explanation: Cost estimation: runs after plan, before apply. Shows: prior monthly estimate, new monthly estimate, delta (change in cost). Uses public pricing APIs. Not 100% accurate (reserved pricing, volume discounts not considered). Integrates with Sentinel: can block applies that exceed cost thresholds.

questions.question: A Terraform configuration creates an S3 bucket using `count = 3`. After applying, you add a fourth bucket by changing `count = 4`. Which bucket resource is created without modifying any existing ones?
options: All four buckets are destroyed and recreated
Only `aws_s3_bucket.example[3]` is created — Terraform adds the new index without touching existing ones
The bucket at index 0 is destroyed and `aws_s3_bucket.example[0]` through `[3]` are created from scratch
Terraform imports the existing three buckets and then creates the fourth without a plan step
questions.explanation: When you increase `count`, Terraform calculates the diff and only adds the new index. `aws_s3_bucket.example[0]`, `[1]`, and `[2]` already exist in state and match the configuration — they are untouched. Only `aws_s3_bucket.example[3]` is planned as a `+create`. This is why `for_each` with stable keys is preferred over `count` for resource sets — inserting an item in the middle with `count` renumbers indexes and triggers unwanted destroys.

questions.question: You have an existing EC2 instance (`i-0abcd1234`) that was created manually and you need to bring it under Terraform management. Which command imports it into the state file?
questions.explanation: `terraform import <resource_address> <provider_id>` is the correct command. It adds the existing resource to the Terraform state without creating or destroying it. You still need to write the corresponding `resource` block in your `.tf` file before running `import`. Terraform does NOT generate the configuration for you (use `terraform plan` after import to verify alignment). `state push` uploads a state file. `refresh` updates state from the real infrastructure but doesn't import new resources.

questions.question: You want to prevent a production database from being accidentally destroyed via `terraform destroy` or a plan that removes it. Which lifecycle configuration achieves this?
options: Set `lifecycle { ignore_changes = all }` — this tells Terraform to ignore drift on all attributes but does not prevent deletion; it does not raise a plan error when a destroy is attempted
Set the resource as `data` instead of `resource` to make it read-only and undeletable by Terraform
Set `lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }` to ensure a new instance is created before the old one is removed
Set `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` — Terraform will error if a plan would destroy this resource
questions.explanation: `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` causes Terraform to return an error if the execution plan would destroy that resource — even in `terraform destroy`. This is a safeguard for critical infrastructure. Note: it only prevents plans that destroy the resource; you can still override it by removing the `prevent_destroy` block and re-running. `ignore_changes = all` prevents Terraform from updating the resource but doesn't prevent destruction. `create_before_destroy` changes the replacement order.

questions.question: A Terraform module in your configuration needs to use the same AWS provider as the root module but targeting a different region. How do you correctly pass a provider alias to the module?
options: Set `region = var.region` in the module provider block — modules cannot declare their own provider blocks when called from a root module; the root module must pass provider aliases via the `providers` meta-argument

Set `AWS_REGION=us-west-2` as an environment variable — this configures the provider region globally for all instances; it cannot selectively pass a specific provider alias to a module that needs a different region
Use the `providers` meta-argument in the module block to map the module's provider alias to the root provider alias
Create a new `provider` block inside the module with the target region — modules auto-detect parent providers
questions.explanation: To pass a non-default provider (an aliased provider) to a module, use the `providers` meta-argument in the calling `module` block: `providers = { aws = aws.us-west-2 }`. This maps the child module's `aws` provider to the parent's `aws.us-west-2` alias. Modules should not define their own provider blocks in most cases (it creates a separate provider instance). Environment variables apply globally, not per-module. Passing region as a variable works but requires explicit provider configuration inside the module.

questions.question: Your team wants to move a Terraform resource from one module path to another without destroying and recreating it. What is the correct approach in Terraform 1.1+?
options: Use `terraform state mv <old_address> <new_address>` to update the state with the new module path
Delete the resource from state with `terraform state rm` and re-import it at the new address
Add a `moved` block in the Terraform configuration that declaratively maps the old address to the new one
Manually edit the `terraform.tfstate` file to update the resource address path
questions.explanation: Terraform 1.1 introduced the `moved` block — a declarative, code-reviewable way to refactor resource addresses without destroying infrastructure. Syntax: `moved { from = module.old.aws_instance.web; to = module.new.aws_instance.web }`. Terraform processes this during `plan`/`apply` and updates the state. `terraform state mv` works but is an imperative CLI command not tracked in version control. Editing the state file directly is dangerous and unsupported.

questions.question: You need to create a dynamic number of security group rules from a list of CIDR blocks. Which Terraform feature creates multiple nested blocks within a resource without code repetition?
options: Use a `dynamic` block with a `for_each` argument to iterate over the CIDR list and generate each rule block

Use a `for` expression to generate a map — this produces a data structure but cannot directly generate repeated nested blocks inside a resource; a `dynamic` block with `for_each` is the correct way to iterate over the CIDR list
Use `templatefile()` function to render the nested blocks as a string and pass them to the resource
Use `count` on the security group resource itself to create one rule per security group instance
questions.explanation: `dynamic` blocks allow you to generate a variable number of nested blocks within a resource. Syntax: `dynamic "ingress" { for_each = var.cidr_list; content { cidr_blocks = [ingress.value] } }`. The `content` block defines the structure of each generated block, and `ingress.value` (or `ingress.key`) accesses the iterator. `for` expressions produce values/maps but can't generate nested blocks. `count` applies to the resource level, not nested blocks. `templatefile()` generates strings, not HCL blocks.

questions.question: You have two resources where resource B needs an attribute from resource A that is only known after `apply` (not during `plan`). What happens during `terraform plan`?
options: Terraform fails the plan with an error since unknown values cannot be used in dependent resources
Terraform shows `(known after apply)` for the dependent attribute in the plan and defers the final value to
Terraform requires you to use `depends_on` explicitly to handle unknown values across resources
questions.explanation: Terraform displays `(known after apply)` in the plan output for any attribute that depends on a value that the provider doesn't know until the resource is created (e.g., an auto-generated ID, an IP address assigned by the cloud). The plan still proceeds — Terraform knows the resource will be created and can reason about the dependency. The final value is resolved during `apply`. `depends_on` is for implicit dependencies where Terraform cannot detect the dependency automatically, not for handling unknown values.

questions.question: In Terraform 0.15+, `terraform taint` was deprecated. What is the recommended replacement to force recreation of a specific resource?
options: Edit the resource configuration and add a dummy `triggers` variable to force a plan change
Use `terraform apply -replace=<resource_address>` to force the resource to be destroyed and recreated
Delete the resource from the state file with `terraform state rm` and run `terraform apply`
questions.explanation: `terraform apply -replace=<resource_address>` (available since Terraform 0.15.2) is the direct replacement for `terraform taint`. It marks the specified resource for replacement in the same apply run, rather than as a separate two-step taint + apply. `terraform taint` still works but is deprecated. `destroy -target` then `apply -target` works but is a two-step manual process. `state rm` followed by `apply` re-creates the resource but loses the import context.

questions.question: Your Terraform Cloud workspace uses a remote backend. You run `terraform plan` locally — what happens to the plan execution?
options: The plan is uploaded to Terraform Cloud and executed there, streaming logs back to your terminal
Terraform Cloud rejects the local plan and requires you to use the web UI to trigger runs
The plan runs locally on your machine using your local credentials and state is synced to Terraform Cloud after
The plan runs locally but uses the Terraform Cloud API to fetch the current state for comparison
questions.explanation: When using the Terraform Cloud remote backend (or HCP Terraform), running `terraform plan` locally sends the configuration to Terraform Cloud, which executes the plan in a managed runner on the Terraform Cloud infrastructure. Logs are streamed back to your terminal in real time. This ensures consistent execution environment, access to workspace variables/secrets, and run history. Plans do not execute locally when using the remote backend — your credentials are not used directly.

questions.question: You use `for_each = toset(["us-east-1", "us-west-2"])` to create resources in two regions. Later you remove `"us-east-1"` from the set. What does Terraform do?
options: Terraform destroys the `us-east-1` resource instance and leaves `us-west-2` unchanged
Terraform fails the plan with an error because removing a `for_each` key requires a manual state rm first
Terraform rebuilds both resources since the set order changed
Terraform creates a new resource for `us-west-2` and orphans the `us-east-1` instance in state
questions.explanation: With `for_each`, each resource instance is keyed by the map key or set value. Removing `"us-east-1"` from the set means that key no longer exists in the configuration. Terraform's diff detects that `resource.example["us-east-1"]` exists in state but not in the new config, so it plans a destroy for that instance only. `resource.example["us-west-2"]` is unchanged. This is a key advantage of `for_each` over `count` — removal doesn't cause index renumbering and unintended replacements of other instances.

questions.question: You inherit a Terraform project that stores state in a local file. Which TWO of the following are valid reasons to migrate the state to a remote backend like S3 + DynamoDB?
options: Concurrent applies from two engineers will be safely blocked by state locking
Terraform will automatically encrypt resource attributes in transit between providers
State is stored off the developer's laptop, surviving a disk failure
Remote backends remove the need to write any provider authentication credentials
questions.explanation: Remote backends (S3+DDB, Terraform Cloud, etc.) provide state locking — preventing the classic "two applies racing" bug. They also persist state outside any one engineer's laptop. Backends do NOT change provider transport encryption (TLS is the provider's job) and you still need provider credentials.
